opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest shift is that you stop optimizing for a single good answer and start optimizing for a long trajectory. A chat model mostly needs to get one response right. An agent has to read tool outputs, keep track of state, recover from its own mistakes, and keep going for dozens or even hundreds of steps. That changes what you care about at almost every level of the architecture.

The first thing is context. Agent workloads are extremely long-context and very prefill-heavy. Every tool call returns a pile of tokens: logs, web pages, file contents. Most of it is only half-relevant, but the model still has to carry it forward. So efficiency in long context stops being a nice-to-have. Attention cost, KV cache size and memory bandwidth become first-order design constraints. That's why you see so much interest in things like sparse attention, hybrid attention, and more aggressive KV compression. If your cost per step is high, a 200-step task just isn't economically viable, no matter how smart the model is.

The second thing is inference speed and the decode side. Agents are interactive loops, so latency compounds. If each step is a bit slow, the whole task becomes painfully slow. So you think about things like multi-token prediction, speculative decoding, and how well the architecture plays with your serving stack. You're co-designing the model and the inference system together much more than before.

Third, and I think this is underrated, the architecture has to be friendly to reinforcement learning at scale. Most agentic capability now comes from RL on long-horizon tasks. Rollouts are expensive and long, and stability really matters. For example, with MoE models you have to watch for mismatches between training and inference, like routing behaving differently in the rollout engine versus the trainer. Small numerical inconsistencies that didn't matter for pretraining can blow up during long RL runs. So "is this architecture stable and consistent under RL" becomes a real selection criterion.

And finally there's a kind of philosophical shift. For a long time the question was "how do we make the model know more." For agents the question is closer to "how do we make the model act well over time with limited compute." Raw knowledge still matters, but the model's ability to use context, use tools, and stay coherent is what separates a good agent from a good chatbot. So I'd say agents push you to think about the whole system, meaning the architecture, the inference engine and the RL pipeline, as one thing rather than designing the model in isolation.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the honest answer is that it changes almost everything downstream of the base model, and it changes a few things upstream too.

Let me start with what an agent model actually has to do differently. A chat model produces a response, the user reads it, and the episode is over. An agent model has to run for a long time, call tools, read back results that are often messy or wrong, and keep track of a goal across dozens or hundreds of steps. So the thing you're optimizing is no longer "is this one answer good," it's "does this whole trajectory succeed." That shift sounds simple but it ripples into the architecture in several ways.

The first is context. Agent trajectories are long, and most of the tokens in them are tool outputs, not model outputs. So you suddenly care enormously about how efficiently the model can consume long inputs. That pushes you toward architectures where the cost of attending over long context is manageable, things like sparse or compressed attention, more aggressive KV cache sharing, and in general treating prefill efficiency as a first-class design goal rather than an afterthought. When we were working on DeepSeek, things like MLA were motivated partly by inference cost, but once you go to agents the pressure becomes much stronger because the ratio of input to output tokens flips.

The second is latency and the shape of inference. For a chat model, you can tolerate a slower, bigger model because the human is the bottleneck. For an agent, the model is in a loop with itself. If each step takes a few seconds and you have a hundred steps, the whole task becomes unusable. So you start to think seriously about mixture-of-experts, about how many active parameters you really need per token, about whether you can make the model cheap per step while keeping total capability high. The architecture becomes a question of amortized cost over a trajectory rather than cost per answer.

The third, and I think this is underappreciated, is that the training signal changes, and that feeds back into architecture. With agents, your data is interactive. You generate rollouts in environments, you get rewards at the end or at checkpoints, and you do reinforcement learning on that. This means your training infrastructure has to support very long rollouts, asynchronous generation, and a lot of inference during training. So the architecture has to be friendly to both training and sampling at the same time. Some design choices that look good on a pure pretraining benchmark turn out to be painful once you need to sample millions of long trajectories. You find yourself choosing designs that keep inference and training on the same hardware path, because otherwise the RL loop becomes the bottleneck of your entire organization.

There's also a question about what the model needs to be good at natively versus what you put in the scaffold around it. Early on, people built a lot of agent behavior in the harness, with retries, planners, memory systems. My view has shifted toward putting more of that capability into the model itself through training, because the model can learn when to retry, when to verify, when to stop, in ways that are hard to hand-code. But that only works if the architecture gives the model enough working memory and enough stable long-horizon behavior. So you end up caring about things like how the model handles very long reasoning without drifting, and whether it can reliably follow a plan it made two hundred steps ago.

And then one more practical thing. Agents make mistakes that compound. A chat model that's wrong once is wrong once. An agent that misreads a tool result may spend fifty steps going in the wrong direction. So robustness to noisy input and the ability to recover become architectural concerns, not just training concerns. You want the model to maintain a kind of uncertainty about its own earlier conclusions. We're still figuring out how much of that is architecture and how much is data, but I don't think you can separate them cleanly anymore.

So if I had to summarize, building agent models forces you to design for the trajectory, not the token. That means long context efficiency, cheap per-step inference, a training stack where sampling is as important as gradient steps, and a model that's stable over long horizons. Those priorities are quite different from what drove a lot of earlier architecture work, and I think the field is still adjusting to them.

astra-6.text:
I think building agent models changes what we optimize for. It’s no longer just, “Can the model give a good answer to this prompt?” It’s, “Can it carry out a task over many steps, use tools, and recover when something goes wrong?” That changes how you think about the architecture.

For example, long context becomes more important, but simply making the context window larger isn’t enough. You need to decide what information to keep, what to retrieve, and how to represent the state of an unfinished task. And inference efficiency matters differently: an agent may call the model dozens of times, so a small cost or latency increase gets multiplied across the whole workflow.

There’s also a boundary to decide between the model and the surrounding system. Which behaviors should the model learn, and which should be handled by explicit orchestration? I don’t think every capability needs a new architectural component. You want to look at where the agent actually fails—whether it loses track of its goal, misuses a tool, or can’t recognize an error—and let those failures guide the design.

So for me, the biggest shift is that the unit of design becomes the whole task, rather than a single response.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest change is that you’re no longer designing a model just to answer a question. You’re designing it to act, observe what happened, and decide what to do next. So architectural decisions have to support that whole loop.

For example, what should live inside the model, and what should be handled by tools or external memory? You probably don’t want every piece of knowledge or every intermediate result in the model’s context. But the model does need to understand when to retrieve information, when to use a tool, and whether the result actually helps it finish the task.

It also changes how you think about efficiency. A slightly better answer per step may not be worth it if each step is very expensive and the agent needs hundreds of them. You care about the cost and reliability of completing the whole task. That pushes you to design the model, the inference system, and the training process together.
